text: White House pulls Overton nomination
The White House has dropped its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official told the Guardian.

Donald Trump nominated Overton – a physician and prominent abortion opponent – in August. But Overton faced a challenging path to Senate confirmation, particularly after Republican senator Bill Cassidy said today that he remained undecided about her nomination ahead of a Senate health, labor and pensions committee vote scheduled for tomorrow.

Marco Rubio said there is “no evidence” that any of the many outages this week “are related to each other” or “with nefarious actors.” The secretary of state made the remarks to reporters while traveling with the president in the Philippines today.
“We have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other,” said Rubio.

He added, “We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind.”
A prominent reproductive rights group celebrated the White House’s decision to pull its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

“Heidi Overton posed a serious threat to the future of medication abortion access. Voters rejected that anti-abortion agenda nationwide, and our members kept the pressure on to tank her confirmation. If Republicans try to rush through another nominee who threatens our healthcare, we’re ready to keep fighting,” said Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All (formerly NARAL Pro-Choice America).

As head of the FDA, Overton would have of overseen the agency that regulates medication abortions. In a 2023 policy brief for the conservative America First Policy Institute, Overton said Congress should strictly regulate the abortion pill mifeprestone “to protect women and children”, criticized federal policies that allow for the mailing of abortion pills and wrote that abortion “is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly”.

A number of lawmakers have raised concerns about a spat of outages over the past week, offered their perspective on what may be happening and called for increased regulations on artificial intelligence and tech companies.

“Over the last week, we’ve heard A LOT about ‘system outages’ from government agencies such as the FAA and NSA, as well as major companies like Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase. We don’t know the full story yet, but the chaos makes one thing obvious: Letting a handful of tech giants control this industry is just too dangerous,” said congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat from Washington state.

“At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort. What appears to be happening instead is a consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape,” Mark Warner, a Democratic senator from Virginia, said in a social media post. “While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

“The American people can see everything happening with these service outages, and they feel like they’re not getting the whole story. You can’t blame anybody for that. I’m a member of Congress, and I feel that way!” said senator Rick Scott, a Republican from Florida. “We need congressional briefings. These companies and federal agencies need to be fully transparent about what’s going on.”

“We don’t yet know what has caused recent outages at major companies and government agencies. We do know that advanced AI threatens to undermine cybersecurity for systems that make our hospitals, banks, and government run. And that could make these sort of outages much more common and damaging,” said congressman Greg Casar of Texas, who called for increased regulations on artificial intelligence.
Donald Trump has nominated Gen Chris LaNeve to be the US army’s top officer, making permanent his interim service after defense secretary Pete Hegseth unexpectedly fired his predecessor in April.
LaNeve had been serving as Hegseth’s senior military commander before his nomination for a fourth star and service as vice chief of staff of the army in February.
My colleague George Chidi has the full story:
Democrat Raymond Smith has won his race to represent North Carolina’s 3rd district in the House of Representatives. Smith beat out the Republican incumbent Greg Murphy in a narrow race.
The Associated Press has yet to call seven other House races and the Alaska Senate race as votes are still being counted from this month’s midterm elections.
Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chair of the company’s board said Tuesday.
Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago.
My colleague Dara Kerr has the full story:

The Board of Peace, which is overseeing the US-brokered ceasefire in Gaza, told the United Nations Security Council today that the ceasefire will collapse if steps are not taken to uphold the full peace agreement.

“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” says the report, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press.

It adds, “Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” calling for immediate “scaled-up entry of shelter and winterization materials.”
The Board delivered its first report to the United Nations in May, at which time it warned: “A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
Defense secretary Pete Hegseth said the Pentagon “will pass a full, clean audit by 2028” in response to news that the defense department failed a financial audit for the ninth year in a row.

The Defense Department was first audited in 2018 and given 10 years to pass an annual audit. An inspector general report released yesterday showed the agency had failed audit again for fiscal year 2026. The news comes as the Trump administration is seeking a record $1.5tn for defense spending.
Despite failing the audit, Hegseth wrote in a social media post: “We are more than halfway there – huge, historic progress so far.”

As defense department CFO Jules Hurst told ⁠Reuters, a majority of the Pentagon’s units passed audit for the first time. According to Hurst, 14 of the Pentagon’s 25 stand-alone reporting entities passed audit in the 2026 fiscal year, up from ⁠11 the prior year.
Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
In late October, a federal magistrate judge ordered Trump to sit for a deposition by BBC lawyers by 11 December. But on Tuesday, a federal district court judge extended the deadline until 22 January.
My colleague Jeremy Barr has the full story:
Lisa Cook, the Federal Reserve governor that Donald Trump has sought to fire since August 2025, has declined to appear before a Trump administration committee next month.
Cook’s attorneys declined the appearance, saying the committee considering whether she should be fired is committed to a predetermined outcome.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing – and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf.

Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine skeptic, said the United States will work to regain measles elimination status and blamed “worldwide COVID-era disruptions” for interrupting routine childhood vacccination.

“Worldwide COVID-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad. The multi-year global outbreak has caused many nations to lose their elimination status including, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Canada, Mexico, Spain, United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan,” Kennedy said in a social media post.

Kennedy – who has overseen the Centers for Disease Control losing up to one-third of its staff, interfered in the agency’s reporting of measles deaths and has spread misinformation about the measles vaccines – added, “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
As my colleague Jessica Glenza reported last week:

The second Trump administration also made broad changes that challenge measles elimination globally. Some of Trump’s first acts in 2024 included withdrawal from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Global Vaccine Alliance (GAVI). GAVI provides measles vaccines to nations such as India and Malawi. There are about 95,000 measles deaths globally, according to the World Health Organization, mostly in unvaccinated children under five years old.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business that a recent string of tech outages are likely due to system upgrades and not a cyber attack.

“Everybody recognizes it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” Clayton told the ⁠Claman Countdown program on Fox Business today.
He added, “Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident.”

Apple reported three outages today, amid a rash of high profile outages in recent days affecting government and private companies. Users are also reporting outages at Marriott International, the largest hotel operator in the US, the Associated Press reports.

Apple reported that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services experienced full outages today. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement to the AP. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
The AP also noted that users posting on Reddit and Downdetector.com reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage. The hotel chain did not immediately respond to an email inquiry from the AP.

Markwayne Mulline, the homeland security secretary, defended his decision to fly to a college football game on Saturday by private government plane, as Americans weathered widespread flight delays and cancellations.
In an interview with CNBC the former Oklahoma senator said, “We still got to live our life.”
Mullin traveled on a government aircraft on Saturday to watch a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas, the New York Post reported on Tuesday.
My colleague Sam Levine has the full story:
Trump brushes off reports of NSA internal network outage: 'it's fine'
Donald Trump brushed off reports that the National Security Agency’s internal network is down in remarks to reporters in Manila today, saying “it’s fine.”
“It’s like when you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said.
As we reported earlier, an NSA spokesperson told the Guardian the outage was the result of “scheduled routine maintenance.”
But after a series of high profile outages over the past week – affecting banks, air traffic control, United Airlines and Microsoft – some have begun to raise concerns.
“If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world,” Republican senator Josh Hawley told reporters today.
Here's a recap of the day so far

The outage of a highly classified internal network at the National Security Agency (NSA), was the result of “scheduled routine maintenance,” an NSA spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement. NSA Net, the network that allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally, was down today, according to several reports. While sources sources told CNN that there was no evidence of a cyber-attack, it is the latest disruption in a series of outages over the last week that have affected the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft, Chase Bank and JP Morgan.

Chuck Schumer again insisted today that he has the votes to secure the leadership position when Democrats take the majority in the new year. “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader, I have the votes, and we’re all going to roll up our sleeves, and we are going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption. Those are the things we’re focused on,” he said, without addressing what the challenge from Senator Chris Van Hollen, a progressive, says about faith in Schumer’s leadership. “We are all united together,” Schumer said, despite the fact that several members of the caucus have pledged support for Van Hollen.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said he’s making “a nice ask” for an additional $50bn in funding for air safety upgrades following the nationwide ground-stop of thousands of flights last week. Several Democrats have slammed the request, arguing that the Republicans guaranteed a $12.5bn air traffic control package last year, and only $1bn has been spent and $8bn has yet to be obligated.

Duffy also said today the FBI is now assisting the investigation into the newly-installed router responsible for the grounding. However, he told reporters today that the US intelligence agencies have assured him the issues were not the result of a cyber-attack. “I think it’s important that we have all precautions. So I asked Kash [Patel] to send me part of his FBI team to be part of the analyzing of this router,” Duffy said.

Hung Cao, who currently serves as the acting Navy secretary, faced lawmakers on the Senate armed services committee to be confirmed as the branch’s permanent top official. During his hearing today, Cao said the eight suicide attempts on board the USS Abraham Lincoln – during a record-breaking deployment– were actually “suicide mitigations”, and defended conditions on the warship. More here and here
Jensen Huang, the embattled former CEO of Nvidia, will appear before House lawmakers on three key committees on 1 December. Huang will appear alongside Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter.

Meanwhile, two departments have confirmed they are investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia’s chips to China. A joint statement issued by the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice explains that Megaspeed has been under investigation since 2024, for “potential export control violations.”

Earlier, in Manila, Donald Trump said that US authorities take “very seriously” any possible threat to Washington, following reports Iran was planning to target officials, possibly with a radioactive bomb. “If there is [such a threat], they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before,” the president said. “I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
Duffy says nationwide grounding was not result of a cyber hack but FBI is assisting investigation into router malfunction
Sean Duffy said today that the US intelligence agencies have assured him the decision to ground of all thousands of flights last week was not the result of a cyber-attack.
However, the FBI is now assisting the investigation into the newly-installed router responsible for the malfunction.

“I think it’s important that we have all precautions. So I asked Kash [Patel] to send me part of his FBI team to be part of the analyzing of this router,” Duffy said. “If we were subject to a hack, we will share that with you as well, but all of my intelligence partners are telling me that wasn’t the case. But again, we have the FBI there partnering with us as we work through this analysis.”
Duffy noted today that he’s making “a nice ask” for an additional $50bn in funding for air safety upgrades, but said he would wait and see how Congress works to allocate the funding.

“Whether it’s on a party line vote or if it’s a bipartisan vote, I do think this is this is one moment in a very charged political environment … where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in and do it. So how they do their work, we’ll watch that together,” he told reporters today.
